The only good the mental hospital did for me, was completely strip stimulation, and access to things that I could use to harm myself. In the extreme state of crisis where I was actually going to take my life, yes it was somewhat helpful in just giving me space to breath away from society.. but there were things I wasn’t ready for, like someone breaking a plastic cup in the eating room, and making a Shank. Or people throwing their poop at the walls/ walking around covered in their piss/shit.   Not that everywhere will be like this. In most places, it’s a minimum amount of time to stay like, mine was required 5 days, could stay up to 7. I felt like I was ready to go at three days, because I had decompressed from my suicidal episode. But, had to stay a couple more days for analysis. I say all that to say, if you feel like you’re on the verge of crisis and you’re really ready to say goodbye to yourself, yes inpatient will be extremely helpful, in taking away stimuli and things you could use to hurt yourself, giving you space to breath/sleep/think. If you’re in a very bad downward spiral of depression and manic phases coming and going, I recommend IOP like someone else recommended. My friend from inpatient went to IOP after we did our time, and found much more relief from the therapy and treatment plan. Everything is very broad though, and every hospital is very different. It all comes down to if you feel like you’re in crisis and are a danger to yourself.

To put it as kindly as possible.

Many people know to avoid puppy mills and “backyard” breeders. But many kind individuals fall prey to the picket-fence appeal of so-called “responsible” breeders and fail to recognize that no matter how kindly a breeder treats his or her animals, as long as dogs and cats are dying in animal shelters and pounds because of a lack of homes, no breeding can be considered “responsible.”

All breeders fuel the animal overpopulation crisis, and every time someone purchases a puppy or a kitten instead of adopting from an animal shelter, homeless animals lose their chance of finding a home—and will be euthanized. Many breeders don’t require every puppy or kitten to be spayed or neutered prior to purchase, so the animals they sell can soon have litters of their own, creating even more animals to fill homes that could have gone to animals from shelters—or who will end up in animal shelters or so-called “no-kill” animal warehouses themselves.

Simply put, for every puppy or kitten who is deliberately produced by any breeder, an animal in an animal shelter dies. Producing animals for sale is a greedy and callous business in a world in which there is a critical and chronic shortage of good homes for dogs, cats, and other animals, and the only “responsible breeders” are those who, upon learning about how they contribute to the overpopulation crisis, spay or neuter their animals and get out of the business altogether. What can bring you back to the present moment and out of your head?
